title: Reasoning primer: syllogisms and the fallacies that imitate them
question: Which of these arguments actually deduce their conclusions — and which only look like they do?

human.label: human
human.definition: A member of the species Homo sapiens.

philosopher.label: philosopher
philosopher.definition: One who pursues wisdom by reasoned inquiry.

wise.label: wise
wise.definition: Having sound judgement grounded in knowledge.

raining.label: raining
raining.definition: Water is falling from clouds at the place and time in question.

fire.label: fire
fire.definition: Combustion producing flame and heat at the place in question.

smoke.label: smoke
smoke.definition: Visible suspended particles produced by combustion.

bank_river.label: riverbank
bank_river.definition: The sloping land alongside a river.

bank_finance.label: financial bank
bank_finance.definition: An institution that holds deposits and lends money.

ground.label: the ground
ground.definition: The surface of the earth at the place in question.

propositions.text: If it is raining today, the ground is wet.
If Socrates is a philosopher, then Socrates is wise.
If there is a fire in the kitchen, there is smoke in the kitchen.
There is no fire in the kitchen.
There is no smoke in the kitchen.
Every swan observed in Europe has been white.

arguments.title: Barbara: Socrates is mortal
arguments.warrant: Universal instantiation of C1 at Socrates, then modus ponens with C2.

arguments.title: Modus ponens: the ground is wet
arguments.warrant: The conditional R1 and its antecedent R2 yield the consequent.

arguments.title: Hypothetical syllogism: every Greek is mortal
arguments.warrant: Chaining two universal conditionals through the shared middle term 'human'.

arguments.title: Two-step chain: Socrates is mortal via being Greek
arguments.warrant: Greek(socrates) gives human(socrates) by C4, which gives mortal(socrates) by C1 — two rule applications, not one.

arguments.title: Affirming the consequent
arguments.warrant: Runs the conditional backwards: from the consequent to the antecedent.

arguments.title: Denying the antecedent
arguments.warrant: Infers the negation of the consequent from the negation of the antecedent.

arguments.title: Undistributed middle
arguments.warrant: Both premises predicate 'human' of their subjects; the middle term is never taken universally, so Greeks and philosophers are never connected.

arguments.title: Equivocation on 'bank'
arguments.warrant: Looks like Barbara, but 'bank' names a riverbank in E1 and a financial institution in E2.

arguments.title: Hasty generalisation: all swans are white
arguments.warrant: Every observed swan was white, so all swans are white.

fallacies.name: affirming_the_consequent
fallacies.explanation: S1 licenses wise from philosopher, not philosopher from wise: Socrates could be wise for other reasons.

fallacies.name: denying_the_antecedent
fallacies.explanation: F1 says fire suffices for smoke, not that it is necessary: smoke could come from burnt toast.

fallacies.name: undistributed_middle
fallacies.explanation: 'Human' is the predicate of both premises and distributed in neither, so nothing links Greeks to philosophers.

fallacies.name: equivocation
fallacies.explanation: The word 'bank' shifts sense between the premises; once each sense is written as its own predicate, the conclusion no longer follows.

fallacies.name: hasty_generalization
fallacies.explanation: European observations do not cover the population the conclusion ranges over; black swans live in Australia.
